title: A Decade In, zeroRISC Sees A Bright Future For Open Silicon
author: Jeff Burt
text:

A Decade In, zeroRISC Sees A Bright Future For Open Silicon

Jeff Burt

Jeff
Burt

Published
thu 15 Oct 2026 // 13:50 UTC

At the Hot Chips conference in 2018, Google hardware engineers detailed their recently introduced “Titan” chip, which was designed to create a silicon root of trust (RoT) in servers. RoT is part of a larger push by processor designers at the time to ensure security in the wake of the Spectre and Meltdown vulnerabilities. They also talked about plans to make it available as an open source offering, another step in the nascent open-silicon movement.Leading the charge on OpenTitan for Google at the time was Dominic Rizzo, who pushed the effort and served as its technical lead manager for five years.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

“The way I sold OpenTitan inside Google was they were buying a lot of heterogenous hardware for the cloud and it made their security posture a little lumpy,” Rizzo tells The Next Platform. “OpenTitan was really the first truly credible, well-resourced, do-it-right-from-scratch open source silicon project.”For Rizzo, it was the starting point for what has become decade-long effort to push the open silicon rock up the hill. He left Google in 2023 but continues to be the project director for OpenTitan for lowRISC, the official maintainer and host of OpenTitan. The same year he departed Google, Rizzo co-founded and is now the CEO of zeroRISC, a startup aimed at pushing for broad commercial adoption of open silicon RoT.In May, zeroRISC – along with other industry players, including Qualcomm, Analog Devices, and Meta, and the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy – launched Pavona under the auspices of GlobalPlatform, a nonprofit standards consortium. Pavona – which Rizzo chairs – is a neutral ecosystem for designing open and secure hardware, similar to how the open source Yocto Project and Zephyr Project work for software. Pavona includes a production-stage post-quantum cryptography (PQC) stack that supports various algorithms, including ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, and a composable platform organization can use to build hardware RoTs and chip subsystems.The arguments for open silicon essentially dovetail with those for open source software, he says. Those include reducing costs by eliminating licensing fees and royalties that come with commercial chips from the likes of Intel, AMD, and Nvidia, reusing infrastructure, and providing better collaboration. Innovation can be faster, greater transparency and trust throughout the supply chain, and having more people involved in the design, which can mean more eyes to detect and fix vulnerabilities and defects.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

The idea of open source silicon rose about the same time as open source software and Linux became a thing, Rizzo says. It just couldn’t get momentum behind it.“It has a lot to do with inconsistent interfaces, inconsistent standards, the fact that roles for engineers in the silicon industry are very specific,” he says. “There's a backend production person, there's a layout person, there's an analog person, there's a digital designer, there is a DV person. It's not like software. There is not really that kind of movement within those roles. They get very, very specialized, so this notion of 'there's this open project that does all these things, leverage it how you will,' that never really took off. There's also a lot fewer people who do it than do software.”However, evolution in the semiconductor industry have helped fuel the recent expansion, including the adoption of the IP business model, according to lowRISC.  “All chip designs today are modular, and the vast majority adopt third-party IP from IP vendors like Arm and Synopsys, and foundries like TSMC,” the company wrote earlier this year. “This IP reuse has brought to the industry a major reduction in development cost and time and increase in quality, which are benefits typically associated with open source. ... It is only a small step for silicon vendors to start using open-source IP instead of that from commercial vendors.”

NEXTPLATFORM AD

In addition, the open RISC-V architecture continues to mature since it’s introduction in 2010 and is broadly adopted in embedded systems, with a push being made to carry it over into the datacenter.“RISC-V almost gave permission because RISC-V is an open source instruction set architecture,” Rizzo says. “Even before, when those things were all super proprietary, Arm famously made quite a bit of money off proprietary ISAs, but what that did is ask the natural question: If you've got an open source ISA, why not open source implementation? That's a natural next step. That granting of permission helped a lot as well.”In addition, lowRISC’s Ibex CPU (below) was released in 2019 and is now in various SoC designs.

In 2014, Nuvoton in 2024 brought to market a discrete RoT security chip (below) based on OpenTitan and announced Google’s plans to use it in Chromebooks running ChromeOS.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

In 2025 came the first release Caliptra (below), RoT architecture that includes OpenTitan elements. It was developed through the CHIPS Alliance and Open Compute Project by such vendors as Microsoft, Google, AMD, and Nvidia, and is designed for datacenter-level SoCs.

Over the past few years, the industry has begun to see more companies and industry groups enter it. lowRISC was launched in 2014, and SiFive – which offers custom silicon solutions based on RISC-V – emerged from stealth two years later. The Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions Alliance, or CHERI, was founded in 2024 with a membership that includes Arm, Google, the UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), and, lowRISC. The technology, which aims to protect data stored in hardware memory by building security into hardware.

zeroRISC also focuses on security with what it calls its “silicon trust stack.” The company’s offerings include a Pavona repository and collaboration layer for chip design teams, with version control, review workflows, and build artifacts, continuous integration that includes verification workloads for physical hardware, and post quantum-ready silicon IP. There’s also a provisioning service that includes a line-side server for the datacenter that is backed by a hardware security module (HSM) and management service that offers OEM debugging and over-the-air updates.In May, the company unveiled the open source release of its cryptographic hardware and software stack for both classical and post-quantum environments. It includes a configurable Cryptolib embedded library in its silicon platform that has a programmable asymmetric cryptography coprocessor (ACC) for post-quantum and classical asymmetric algorithms and dedicated hardware accelerators for symmetric operations like AES and SHA2/3.PQC is a key challenge for the industry and organizations like Pavona, according to Rizzo. The U.S. government and its counterparts in Europe and elsewhere are setting aggressive deadlines for organizations to institute such technologies to address the upcoming quantum computing era. Quantum systems are expected to be able to quickly decrypt data that is protected by AES-256 and similar encrypting techniques, and that threat groups with access to such computers will be able to access data they may have already stolen but can yet access, a threat called “harvest now, decrypt later.”Google has placed that time as early as 2029, while others are looking at 2030 or later. Moving to PQC is a significant transition for companies, the type that only comes once in a lifetime or so, and it’s beginning to happen with ML-DSA, MLKEM, and SPHINCS+, with more on the way, Rizzo says.“PQ cryptography, it's a bit more of a pain to implement than the classical cryptography because in classical cryptographic, you have one hard problem that tends to be at the root of all of these pictographic operations and primitives, especially for asymmetric” cryptography, he says. “Post-quantum cryptography does not work the same way and the trade-offs are a lot more varied and the underlying hard problems are different, and then the implementations for the different operations are themselves also different.”Going forward, there are things that need to be address, he says. With Pavona, IP work, like with block design and development, is being done, but a lot of the effort is going into areas like infrastructure, configurability and flexibility that will make it easier for organizations to use open silicon technologies. Governance also is a key issue.“That’s one of the more interesting aspects of this whole thing because we can build the technology in the open,” Rizzo says. “We understand how to do that. It's more like, how do you sustain it for the long term? How do you build the real ecosystem around it? How do you make it so that everyone benefits to some degree, not just a single supporter?”In addition, new regulations like the European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act are shifting the liability for cyber incidents onto the device makers, which is forcing them to look at what they implement and what they take responsibility for, and to dig deeper into their supply chains to ensure they have greater control over what they’re building, he says.“You need to have a hardware root of trust below the software that you can reset back to a known good state or all hope is lost,” Rizzo says. “That’s dawning on people. You need to actually have control over the chips. The software attack surface has always been large, but now the attack capability has grown to match that large surface. The way you address that is you have a silicon root of trust.”
